Insulet Corporation (PODD) Shareholders Who Lost Money Have Opportunity to Lead Securities Fraud Lawsuit

Insulet Corporation (PODD) Shareholders Who Lost Money Have Opportunity to Lead Securities Fraud Lawsuit

PR Newswire

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 21, 2026

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz announces that investors with losses related to Insulet Corporation (PODD) have opportunity to lead the securities fraud class action lawsuit.

IF YOU ARE AN INVESTOR WHO SUFFERED A LOSS IN INSULET CORPORATION (PODD), CLICK HERE BEFORE AUGUST 31, 2026 (THE LEAD PLAINTIFF DEADLINE) TO PARTICIPATE IN THE ONGOING SECURITIES FRAUD LAWSUIT.

What Is The Lawsuit About?
The complaint filed in this class action alleges that between February 21, 2025 and May 26, 2026, Defendants made materially false and/or misleading statements, as well as failed to disclose material adverse facts about the Company's business, operations, and prospects. Specifically, Defendants failed to disclose to investors that: (1) Insulet's manufacturing controls and procedures were defective; (2) the foregoing created a foreseeable heightened risk that one or more Insulet products would be found to be in violation of applicable safety regulations and/or pose a risk of injury; and (3) as a result, Defendants' positive statements about the Company's business, operations, and prospects were materially misleading and/or lacked a reasonable basis at all relevant times.

data.title: 'The estrangement isn't about politics': My daughter hasn't spoken to me for 4 years. Do I leave her a monthly annuity?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'You'll have to trust me when I tell you that she had love, support and opportunities'

"I also believe parents shouldn't give their estranged children the power to negatively control their emotions or lives." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm the guy who wrote to you - and was published - who is 70, still working, loving it, and taking a week off every month ("After 46 years working, I'm not retiring - instead, I take a vacation every month. Is that a good life in your 70s?").

I really appreciate your thoughtful, considered opinions. Your recent letter about the estranged son and daughter-in-law hit home for me ("Our son and daughter-in-law cut us out of their lives after a political argument. Should we change our $3 million will?").

I have four kids - two are mine and two are my wife's - but they are all ours in every meaningful sense. My daughter hasn't spoken to me in four years. She occasionally communicates through Facebook with my previous spouse, with whom I'm still close.

The estrangement isn't about politics. She blames us - and her biological brother - for everything bad that happened to her. You'll have to trust me when I tell you that she had love, support and opportunities above and beyond what most kids receive.

If we ever reconcile, the estate plan can always be changed.

I'm currently rewriting my estate plan. I previously wrote my daughter out of it, but I review my estate plan every couple of years because life changes every couple of years. The letter writer described her decision as irreversible. It isn't irreversible until we die.

We've decided to provide my daughter with a monthly life annuity. She has no children, and the amount will be less than what the others will receive directly. The income will protect the money from her and, potentially, from people around her who might take advantage of her.

If she had children, I would consider structuring the trust to help with things like education or a first home. I'd also make sure there was a corporate trustee or a truly trusted friend involved, because I wouldn't trust my daughter to manage a large inheritance herself.

In my case, the monthly annuity for my estranged daughter will be a reminder, every month for the rest of her life, that her father was still there and still cared about her. If we ever reconcile, the estate plan can always be changed.

Don't miss: I don't want to leave my financially irresponsible daughter my house. Is that unreasonable?

The emotional side

On the emotional side, I believe time can change things. I never give up hope because a father - or mother - always hopes for a better outcome for their children. But I also believe parents shouldn't give their estranged children the power to negatively control their emotions or lives.

At some point, I think the parents have to give the kids exactly what they say they want: total estrangement. Stop trying. Stop sending the messages. Stop chasing them. Let them go. That is incredibly hard, especially when grandchildren are involved.

It's truly a tragedy when families become casualties of things that, in the long run, may not matter nearly as much as the people involved. If my daughter had children and refused to let me see them, I'd handwrite a letter to each grandchild every birthday and/or holiday.

I'd tell them how much I missed them and describe the things we would be doing together if I were allowed to be part of their lives. Most importantly, I'd tell them that I loved them. Then I'd seal and date every letter and put them away.

Stop trying. Stop sending the messages. Stop chasing them.

Maybe someday I'd have the opportunity to give those letters to my grandchildren when they were old enough to understand why they had an absent grandfather. There's a risk they could end up being read at my graveside. So be it.

There's also a risk that doing this could eventually damage my daughter's relationship with her own children. But, honestly, I don't think that would change my decision. The grandchildren deserve to know that they were loved, even if that love had to exist in absentia.

I think that could mean a great deal to them someday. So my advice to the parents who wrote you that letter about falling out with their son and daughter-in-law would be: Give the estranged children what they say they want and leave them alone - truly alone.

And, of course, politics is temporary. Republicans and Democrats will come and go. Time and reality have a way of changing people's perspectives, and I suspect many people will eventually regret some of the choices they made while they were angry.

Father & Husband

Related: 'This is a tricky subject': We're in our 70s and our only child is 40. Do we leave her everything?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Sometimes, the hardest thing to do is to love someone from afar, and support them from afar.

Dear Father,

Thank you for sharing your story.

People do share in great detail here all the time, but yours is deeply personal. I appreciate that your goal is to help others, and assure parents who are going through something similar that it does, indeed, get better. After four years, you are clearly still adjusting to this new normal.

Your advice is sound, particularly as it comes from first-hand experience. It is more painful to chase a relationship - try to fix it and to lie awake thinking about what you could have done differently - than it is to finally accept that it's either over or on pause, and let go.

Letting go is a decision, but it's often a daily practice too, as you have no doubt discovered. What struck me about the father and mother whose son and daughter-in-law cut off contact due to their differences over politics and religion was the finality in his letter.

You are walking a line, knowing that you cannot keep trying to control what someone else does or doesn't do, but also not allowing an experience of loss and frustration to control you. It's not as easy as it seems, especially for someone you love, and I applaud you for that.

Letting go is a decision, a hard one, but it's often also a daily practice.

Sometimes, the hardest thing to do is to love someone from afar, and support them from afar, and quell those feelings of anger and/or confusion that may come up from time to time. Allowing someone space and time is a gift, and it's probably the most selfless kind of gift.

About those letters. Your instinct is right: Express your love for any future grandchildren in writing, but also know that leaving a stash of letters behind could also damage their relationship with their mother and, even if it wasn't your intention, serve as a kind of payback for cutting ties.

Reading between the lines, I feel like you are unsure about putting any grandchildren in the position of having to decipher the past and/or take sides in an adult conflict, especially before they are old enough to do so. "I love you" says everything they need to know.

The letters form a bridge, one that may not allow you to let go completely and free yourself from the more difficult aspects of this estrangement. Setting up a trust and/or bequest is a way you can take action; that can do far more than words, which are open to misinterpretation, can.

Don't miss: Can I claim 50% of my husband's Social Security now - and switch to my higher benefit at 70?

Financial plan

One of the trickiest parts about having an estranged child is dealing with estate planning. Like I said to the previous letter writer, there's no right or wrong way to go about that. Some people write to me and say, "I'll cut them out of my life in every way." And that's their decision.

Others, like you, make plans to provide their estranged child with an income, even a modest one, or make provisions for their grandchildren through a trust or 529 plan. That's generous and it takes not a small amount of magnanimity to put aside hurt feelings like that.

Marital trusts are extremely useful for blended families, so each spouse ensures that their respective children are taken care of if one of them dies. A special-needs trust or spendthrift trust can also distribute funds based on need, including medical bills.

If one child or grandchild decides to go to college, the trust can provide for that. If another child falls off the wagon and needs rehab, the trust could fund that too. The tax benefits help to ensure that a significantly higher portion of your estate passes to your children tax-free.

Sometimes when people feel unhappy, they look for someone to blame.

There are certain actions that give us a semblance of control: writing letters, setting up a monthly annuity, creating a family trust. All of these things come from a good place, but I think it's worth knowing that it can be a way of engaging too.

There are positive (a monthly income) and maybe not-so-positive (writing letters to future grandchildren to be opened upon your death) ways of making sure that your legacy remains. An annuity is a fine idea, but set it up and let it go (until your next estate review).

You mention that you would not fully have faith in your daughter handling a large sum of money and/or believe there's a risk she could be subject to undue influence from a friend or partner, if she did have a lot of money sitting in her bank account.

That tells me that, perhaps, she has some self-reflection to do. And, sometimes, when people feel unhappy or resentful, rather than look at their own choices, they look for people to blame. I'm sorry that you appear to be that person in this situation.

data.title: Game, Set, Pit! Dickey’s Barbecue Launches Mobile Games To Connect with Next Generation of Fans
data.description:
Game, Set, Pit! Dickey’s Barbecue Launches Mobile Games To Connect with Next Generation of Fans

  • Live now on the Dickey’s Mobile App, loyalty members can play games weekly for a chance to score reward points.
  • Memory, Big Yellow Cup Flip Challenge and Catcher are the first three interactive games as part of this loyalty rollout.
  • The new feature reinforces Dickey's investment in digital innovation and customer loyalty while encouraging more guests to engage directly through the Dickey's mobile app.

With nearly 30% of all online orders now placed through the Dickey's mobile app, Dickey's Barbecue Pit is giving guests another reason to tap in. The world's largest barbecue concept announced today the launch of three new interactive mobile games exclusively for Big Yellow Cup Rewards members, allowing fans to earn loyalty points simply by playing, engaging and making every visit to the Dickey's app even more rewarding.

New Mobile App Game Details:

Available now, Big Yellow Cup Rewards members can earn loyalty points while playing three interactive mini games directly within the Dickey's mobile app. The new games, which were a custom development feature by the Spark Adriatic team, includes three distinct ways to play. Each day, one of the following games will be available for users to enjoy and earn points at random:

  • Big Yellow Cup Flip Challenge: Test your skills by flipping Dickey's iconic Big Yellow Cup and landing it upright before time runs out.
  • Memory: Match pairs of Dickey's-themed cards before the clock expires.
  • Catcher: Build the perfect barbecue sandwich by catching falling ingredients within the allotted time.

How to Play:

  • Games can be accessed by tapping the Weekly Challenge on the Home or Rewards tab within the Dickey's mobile app.
  • Rewards members can play one game each day, with games randomized daily.
  • Guests earn loyalty points whether they successfully complete the game or not, making every player a winner.
  • Members can earn up to 30 loyalty points each week by successfully completing all three weekly game challenges.

Big Yellow Cup Rewards:

  • Join Dickey's Big Yellow Cup Rewards to earn points with every purchase and earn exclusive offers, personalized perks and freebies.
  • Loyalty members earn 10 points for each dollar spent.
  • Orders placed through the Dickey’s mobile app are automatically converted to loyalty points.
  • For in-store purchases, guests can scan their personalized QR code located within the app at checkout or enter their receipt information within seven days of purchase to receive reward points.
  • Users can also earn points by completing a survey located on their receipt and entering it through the app under the rewards section.

Laura Rea Dickey, CEO of Dickey's Barbecue Restaurants, Inc., said, "At Dickey's, we're always looking for new ways to make every barbecue experience more rewarding. Our Big Yellow Cup Rewards members are some of our most loyal guests, and these new mobile games give them another fun reason to open the app, engage with our brand and earn rewards they can use toward their next barbecue meal."

FAQ

Q: How do I access the games?
A: Tap the Weekly Challenge from either the Home or Rewards tab inside the Dickey's mobile app.

Q: What games are currently available?
A: Members may receive one of three randomized games: Memory, Big Yellow Cup Flip Challenge or Catcher.

Q: How many games can I play?
A: Guests may play one game per day.

Q: How many loyalty points can I earn?
A: Members can earn up to 30 loyalty points each week by successfully completing all three weekly challenges. Guests also receive points even if they do not complete a game successfully.

Q: Why should I order through the Dickey's mobile app?
A: Ordering directly through Dickey's provides access to Big Yellow Cup Rewards, exclusive member-only offers, lower prices than many third-party delivery platforms, reduced fees and the easiest way to earn loyalty points on every purchase.

To learn more, follow Dickey’s on Facebook, Instagram. Download the Dickey’s Barbecue Pit app from the Apple App Store or Google Play.

About Dickey’s Barbecue Restaurants, Inc.

Dickey's Barbecue Restaurants, Inc., the world’s largest barbecue concept, was founded in 1941 by World War I Veteran, Travis Dickey. For the past 85 years, Dickey’s Barbecue Pit has served millions of guests Legit. Texas. Barbecue™ alongside their iconic Big Yellow Cup. data.title: The Week in Oil: Stalled Hormuz Talks, Trump's Economic Threats Keep Risk Premium High
data.description:
By Giulia Petroni 




  Here's a look at what happened in oil markets in the week of August 17-21 and what the focus will be in the days to come. 





  OVERVIEW: Oil prices are headed for another weekly gain as stalled talks to reopen Hormuz and U.S. threats to launch a major economic campaign against Iran keep the geopolitical risk premium high. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, is trading above $93 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures are at around $86 a barrel. The benchmarks are up 6% and 5% on the week, respectively. 





   MACRO: Investors viewed the U.S. Treasury's plans to expand bond buybacks to lower long-term yields as a sign of stress in the bond market, sparking a fresh round of dollar selling. The move also raised questions about the government's borrowing costs and fiscal position. Meanwhile, markets have scaled back expectations for higher interest rates following recent U.S. economic data. According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders are now pricing in a 65% probability that the Federal Reserve will leave rates unchanged at its next meeting. 





  GEOPOLITICAL RISKS: With talks to end the Iran war showing few signs of progress, the risk of further disruption to regional energy flows continues to support crude and refined product prices. 



  Trump said Wednesday he would launch a major economic campaign against Iran and any entity that does business with the regime, pushing oil prices higher. More details are expected on Monday. 



  "Is there a difference between armed conflict and economic warfare? The market does not think so, as crude oil rallied nearly $2 on the news," Tamas Varga, analyst at brokerage PVM Oil said. "After all, it will not rob Iran of the possibility of retaliating, keeping Hormuz shut, and targeting regional energy infrastructure and shipping." 





  SUPPLY AND DEMAND: Despite the recent rise to around $94 a barrel, oil prices remain well below the annual high of just above $125 reached in late April. Prices have been contained by the various ways Gulf oil exports have continued to reach markets, as well as weak buying from China, according to analysts. 



  Meanwhile, EIA's inventory data show a mixed picture. Crude stocks have recovered over the past two weeks following a substantial build, but supplies of refined products have tightened. Gasoline inventories are about 5% below the seasonal average, while middle-distillate stocks, including diesel and heating oil, are nearly 13% lower. 





  WHAT'S AHEAD: Looking ahead, markets will remain focused on developments around the Strait of Hormuz and their impact on oil supplies. On the economic calendar, attention will turn to the U.S. PCE inflation data, due Wednesday, which could provide fresh clues on the Federal Reserve's interest-rate path. 





  Write to Giulia Petroni at giulia.petroni@wsj.com

data.title: Indiana American Water and American Water Charitable Foundation Support Disaster Recovery Efforts Across Indiana
data.description:
Indiana American Water and American Water Charitable Foundation Support Disaster Recovery Efforts Across Indiana

Indiana American Water and American Water Charitable Foundation Support Disaster Recovery Efforts Across Indiana

PR Newswire

GREENWOOD, Ind., Aug. 21, 2026

$70,000 in funding support to help communities recover from severe storms and flooding, including Northwest Indiana, Muncie, Richmond, Noblesville and Cambridge City

GREENWOOD, Ind., Aug. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Indiana American Water and the American Water Charitable Foundation (AWCF), a philanthropic non-profit organization established by American Water, are providing financial assistance and on-the-ground support to communities impacted by severe storms and flooding across Indiana.

Through a combination of disaster relief grants and strategic community investments, AWCF and Indiana American Water have committed more than $70,000 to organizations assisting residents and families recovering from recent weather-related emergencies. In addition, Indiana American Water employees worked tirelessly throughout the storms, keeping back up power operational and sandbagging facilities to help continue providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable drinking water and wastewater services through the storms.

"When weather events impact Indiana communities, our employees don't hesitate to step up," said Barry L. Suits, President of Indiana American Water. "Whether they're helping maintain critical water and wastewater systems or supporting emergency response efforts -- even when their own families and communities are facing storm-related challenges -- our team remains committed to serving fellow Hoosiers. In addition, we are grateful for the support of the American Wate Charitable Foundation, who helped provide meaningful relief and recovery assistance across Indiana. These grants, combined with the commitment of our employees, reflect our mission to support the health and well-being of the communities we serve."

The American Water Charitable Foundation awarded $55,000 to the American Red Cross to support disaster relief efforts following widespread storm and flood damage across Indiana. This assistance follows an additional $25,000 disaster relief grant provided in June this year to support tornado recovery efforts in the state.

In addition to disaster relief grants, funding was provided through the Foundation's State Strategic Impact Grant Program to support local organizations providing supplemental assistance to residents affected by recent storms and flooding.

Organizations receiving grants include:

  • Legacy Foundation, Merrillville – $5,000 to support local disaster recovery and community assistance efforts in Northwest Indiana.
  • Hamilton County Community Foundation, Noblesville – $5,000 to support flood recovery assistance programs serving Hamilton County residents impacted by recent flooding.

Complementing these relief efforts, Indiana American Water donated $2,500 to both the City of Muncie and the City of Richmond to assist with local response and recovery activities in the aftermath of the flooding.

Beyond financial support, Indiana American Water employees mobilized to help safeguard critical infrastructure and support affected communities throughout the state.

In Northwest Indiana, utility employees worked around the clock to maintain water and wastewater operations during the severe weather conditions. Several employees continued serving customers even while parts of their own communities experienced extended power outages and damage to property.

In Muncie, water operations personnel helped protect critical treatment infrastructure as floodwaters rose by assisting with efforts to secure and safeguard facilities, helping maintain reliable service for customers during the storms.

The company's support also extended beyond its service territory. Indiana American Water deployed a mobile drinking water semi-trailer to Cambridge City to assist local emergency response and recovery efforts, providing an additional resource for neighboring community leaders and first responders as they worked to support residents impacted by flooding.

"These recovery efforts demonstrate the resilience of Indiana communities and the dedication of countless organizations, volunteers and first responders," Suits continued. "We are proud to partner with organizations such as the American Red Cross, Legacy Foundation and Hamilton County Community Foundation to help provide relief and support long-term recovery in the communities we serve and neighboring communities that need assistance."

About American Water
American Water (NYSE: AWK) is the largest regulated water and wastewater utility company in the United States. With a history dating back to 1886 and celebrating 140 years in 2026, We Keep Life Flowing® by providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable drinking water and wastewater services to approximately 14 million people with regulated operations in 14 states and on 19 military installations. American Water's approximately 7,000 talented professionals leverage their significant expertise and the company's national size and scale to achieve excellent outcomes for the benefit of customers, employees, investors and other stakeholders. For more information, visit amwater.com and join American Water on LinkedIn, Facebook, X and Instagram.

About the American Water Charitable Foundation
The American Water Charitable Foundation, a philanthropic non-profit organization established by American Water, focuses on three pillars of giving: Water, People and Communities. Through strategic investments, outreach and volunteerism, the Foundation helps support initiatives that strengthen communities, improve access to clean water and enhance environmental stewardship.

About Indiana American Water
Indiana American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, is the largest regulated water utility in the state, providing high-quality and reliable water and wastewater services to approximately 1.5 million people. For more information, visit amwater.com/inaw and join Indiana American Water on LinkedIn, Facebook, X and Instagram.

data.title: AM Best Affirms Credit Ratings of Jubilee General Insurance Company Limited
data.description:
AM Best Affirms Credit Ratings of Jubilee General Insurance Company Limited

AM Best has affirmed the Financial Strength Rating (FSR) of B (Fair) and the Long-Term Issuer Credit Rating (Long-Term ICR) of “bb” (Fair) of Jubilee General Insurance Company Limited (Jubilee) (Pakistan). The outlook of FSR is stable while the outlook of the Long-Term ICR is positive.

These Credit Ratings (ratings) reflect Jubilee’s balance sheet strength, which AM Best assesses as strong, as well as its strong operating performance, limited business profile and marginal enterprise risk management (ERM).

Jubilee’s balance sheet strength assessment is underpinned by its risk-adjusted capitalisation at the strongest level, as measured by Best’s Capital Adequacy Ratio (BCAR) at year-end 2025. The company’s BCAR scores are projected to improve due to the de-risking of its investment portfolio throughout 2026. The company is targeting a reduction of its equity portfolio to approximately 30% of total investments, down from 43% at year-end 2025, with the proceeds from sales reinvested into fixed income securities. Jubilee’s capital requirements in BCAR are significantly weighted toward asset risk, and therefore its risk-adjusted capitalisation is highly sensitive to changes in asset allocation. Other partially offsetting factors include Jubilee’s high reinsurance dependence and its exposure to a non-rated reinsurance counterparty through mandatory cessions to the state-owned reinsurer in Pakistan.

Jubilee has a history of strong earnings, with a five-year (2021-2025) weighted average return on equity of 19.5%. Underwriting performance has been resilient over this period, with a five-year weighted average combined ratio of 95.4%. The company experienced a poor underwriting year in 2025, evidenced by a 101.3% combined ratio, impacted by large flood losses and fire events. AM Best expects that the company’s prospective underwriting performance will improve following corrective actions taken by management. Investment returns remain the core driver of operating performance, with Jubilee generating a weighted average net investment yield, including capital gains, of 15.8% over the same five-year period.

As the third-largest private non-life insurer in Pakistan, Jubilee holds a solid competitive position within domestic market. The company’s premium income increased by 15.2% in 2025. This was supported by inflation-driven rate increases and higher sums insured. However, writing PKR 26.6 billion (USD 95.0 million) of gross premium in 2025, Jubilee remains relatively small on a global scale.

AM Best views Jubilee’s ERM as marginal given the size and complexity of its operations. The company’s risk profile remains exposed to Pakistan’s elevated economic, political and financial system risks. While AM Best notes Jubilee’s historical operational resilience to country risk factors, risk management challenges are presented by its concentration of business and assets in Pakistan.

Rosen Law Firm, a global investor rights law firm, reminds investors about a class action lawsuit on behalf of purchasers of securities of Photronics, Inc.(NASDAQ: PLAB) between December 10, 2025 and May 27, 2026, inclusive (the “Class Period”). Photronics is a global manufacturer of photomasks.

For more information, submit a form, email attorney Phillip Kim, or give us a call at 866-767-3653.

The Allegations: Rosen Law Firm is Investigating the Allegations that Photronics, Inc.(NASDAQ: PLAB) Misled Investors Regarding its Business Operations.

According to the complaint, defendants provided overwhelmingly positive statements to investors while, at the same time, disseminating materially false and misleading statements and/or concealing material adverse facts concerning the true state of Photronics’ high-end product pipeline, customer schedules, and the stability of the alleged demand for its products; notably, that the seasonal recovery and design release momentum following the Chinese New Year holiday, which Photronics was claiming would develop, had stalled. Photronics was experiencing a critical bottleneck in its design release pipeline that rendered its forward growth expectations unachievable. When the true details entered the market, the lawsuit claims that investors suffered damages.

What Now: You may be eligible to participate in the class action against Photronics, Inc.Shareholders who want to serve as lead plaintiff for the class must file their motions with the court by September 4, 2026. A lead plaintiff is a representative party who acts on behalf of other class members in directing the litigation. You do not have to participate in the case to be eligible for a recovery. If you choose to take no action, you can remain an absent class member. For more information, click here.

All representation is on a contingency fee basis. Shareholders pay no fees or expenses.

About Rosen Law Firm: Some law firms issuing releases about this matter do not actually litigate securities class actions. Rosen Law Firm does. Rosen Law Firm is a recognized leader in shareholder rights litigation, dedicated to helping shareholders recover losses, improving corporate governance structures, and holding company executives accountable for their wrongdoing. Since its inception, Rosen Law Firm has obtained over $2 billion for shareholders.

data.title: ICE Canola Midday: Profit-Taking Spurring Losses
data.description:
Winnipeg -- Profit-taking was pulling down Intercontinental Exchange canola futures lower at mid-session Friday.

An analyst said the speculative funds are "dictating prices" as they have a large long position.

"Come harvest, you don't want to be long," the analyst said.

He warned if the canola market becomes overextended, a great deal of selling will lead to a huge move to the downside.

He also said farmers are doing very well, being adequately sold at this time.

Additional pressure on canola was coming from declines in the Chicago soy complex and European rapeseed, while Malaysian palm oil pushed higher. Crude oil was slightly lower, putting some weight on the vegetable oils.

Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada upped its call on the coming canola harvest by 600,000 tonnes to now 21.6 million. AAFC dropped The carryover for 2026-27 to 1.5 million tonnes from 2.07 million in its July report. Statistics Canada will provide its look at 2026-27 when it scheduled to issue its principal crop report on Sept. 16.

The Canadian dollar was a pinch higher with the loonie at 72.62 U.S. cents late Friday morning, compared to Thursday's close of 72.57.
